question: What does the intravenous route involve delivering substances directly into?

options.D: The digestive tract via the stomach

explanation: Intravenous means inside a vein, allowing direct delivery into the bloodstream for rapid effect. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why is the intravenous route preferred over oral medications during a severe medical emergency?

options.A: It is completely painless for the patient
options.B: It prevents the kidneys from filtering drugs
options.D: It completely avoids the need for a nurse

explanation: Injecting medication directly into the vein skips absorption time, making it act instantly when seconds matter. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h1)

question: What makes intravenous therapy risky regarding how fast drugs act?

options.A: The slow onset of therapeutic effects
options.C: Total immunity to local tissue irritation
options.D: The rapid irreversibility of drug action

explanation: You're doing great! Once a medicine goes straight into the vein, you cannot take it back out. That's why we always double-check our doses—reactions happen fast and are harder to reverse than oral pills. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h2)

question: Why do nurses use continuous IV infusions for certain medications?
explanation: Think of a continuous infusion as a steady drip that keeps the medicine level just right in the body over time, avoiding sudden spikes or drops. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h2)

question: When starting a routine IV line, where should you look first on the patient's arm?

options.A: The most proximal sites on the arm
options.B: The large veins near the neck
options.C: The most distal veins of the hand
options.D: The deep veins close to the core

explanation: Always start down on the hands (distal) and work your way up the arm later if needed. This saves the upper veins for future use! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h3)

question: A patient needs an IV that won't get blocked every time they bend their arm. Which spot should you avoid?
explanation: The antecubital fossa sits right at the inner elbow crease. When the patient bends their arm, the tubing kinks and the pump starts beeping. Better to pick a spot on the forearm or hand! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h3)

question: Which antiseptic is most commonly used to clean the skin before putting in a cannula?
explanation: Chlorhexidine is our go-to skin cleaner for stopping germs and keeping nasty bloodstream infections away. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h4)

question: Why is it important to gather all your IV equipment before you walk to the patient's bedside?

options.A: It prevents the patient from feeling any pain
options.B: It ensures an efficient and organized procedure
options.C: It guarantees the vein will not rupture
options.D: It eliminates the need to wear gloves

explanation: Being prepared keeps you calm, maintains clean technique, and helps the patient feel safe and relaxed while you work. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h4)

question: What tells you right away that your needle has successfully entered the vein?

options.A: The patient reporting a burning sensation
options.B: A flash of blood in the catheter hub
options.C: Sudden swelling around the insertion site
options.D: A complete absence of a distal pulse

explanation: That little flash of dark red blood in the chamber is a nurse's best friend—it lets you know you're right inside the blood vessel! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h5)

question: You see a flash of blood, but when you try to slide the plastic cannula forward, it feels stuck and the patient winces in pain. What likely happened?

options.A: The IV fluid is running at an incorrect rate
options.B: The skin antiseptic was not allowed to dry
options.C: The needle punctured through the back wall of the vein
options.D: The tourniquet was removed too early

explanation: Ah, you might have gone right through the back wall! It happens to everyone when learning. Take a breath, pull back safely, and try a fresh spot. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is the main reason for setting up an IV piggyback (IVPB)?

options.A: To rapidly drain excess blood volume
options.C: To measure direct central venous pressure

explanation: An IV piggyback lets you hang a smaller bag of medicine (like an antibiotic) to run alongside the main IV fluid bag without hassle. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h6)

question: Why must the secondary piggyback medication bag hang higher than the main IV bag?

options.A: It stops the primary line from ever leaking
options.B: It prevents air bubbles from entering the pump
options.C: Gravity pulls fluid from the higher bag first
options.D: It mixes both medications together instantly

explanation: Physics at work! Hanging the secondary bag higher lets gravity pull that medicine through first before the main bag kicks back in. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h6)

question: What unit of measurement do electronic IV infusion pumps typically use to set fluid rates?
explanation: Infusion pumps are programmed directly in mL/hr to deliver precise fluid volumes over time. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h7)

question: Calculate the flow rate: 1000 mL of normal saline over 8 hours using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL.
explanation: Math time! Multiply total volume (1000) by drop factor (15) to get 15,000. Divide by total minutes (480 mins in 8 hours), which gives 31.25—round it down to 31 drops per minute. You've got this! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h7)

question: What are the classic warning signs of phlebitis at an IV site?

options.A: Redness, warmth, and tenderness along the vein
options.B: Complete absence of blood return or fluid flow
options.C: Cool skin and severe swelling without pain
options.D: An immediate drop in the patient's heart rate

explanation: Phlebitis means the vein is irritated or inflamed. Look out for redness, a warm feeling to the touch, and tenderness right along the vein path. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h8)

question: A patient's IV arm feels tight, looks swollen, and feels cool to the touch. What complication has likely happened?
explanation: When IV fluids leak out into the surrounding skin tissue instead of the vein, we call it infiltration. The skin will look pale, swollen, and feel cool. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h8)

question: What is the most important check a nurse must do before starting any IV infusion?

options.A: Verifying the five rights of medication administration
options.B: Ensuring the patient fasts for at least 12 hours
options.C: Checking the patient's deep tendon reflexes
options.D: Obtaining a written surgical consent form from the doctor

explanation: Safety first! Always check the right patient, medication, dose, route, and time every single time before giving any drug. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h9)

question: Why should you encourage patients to tell you immediately if their IV site starts burning?

options.A: It eliminates the need for the nurse to check the pump
options.B: It allows early detection of infiltration or extravasation
options.C: It proves the patient is paying attention to instructions
options.D: It guarantees the medication is working at maximum speed

explanation: Patients are our best partners! If they speak up early about burning or pain, you can stop the infusion before any real damage happens to their skin. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T5#GNS125_U3_T5_h9)
